author: Sophia grey
title: The cruelest season Spanish Edition
text:
Elizabeth
          
        
      
    
    

      
“Mama, it was nothing,” Elizabeth sighed. “Lydia has already told you what happened in great detail, I am certain of that.”

      
“She has, indeed,” Mrs. Bennet cried. “And I wish to know what might have happened to make you believe that it was the best course of action?”

      
Her mother’s shrill tone was, as always, one of Elizabeth’s least favorite sounds. All eyes at the table were turned to her and Elizabeth’s shoulders straightened.

      
“It was raining, Mama,” Elizabeth said gently. “I thought that you would prefer that we returned home without the accompaniment of several pounds of mud upon our gowns and three pairs of ruined shoes.”

      
“You should have checked the almanac,” Mrs. Bennet fumed. She was, of course, not really angry. The exclamations and concern were merely for show. Had they brought the officers in for tea, their mother’s reaction might have been different. But the circumstance had not lent itself to such pleasantries. 

      
 “I did,” Elizabeth sighed. “It has been very temperamental of late. A prediction of rain, but not a cloud in the sky… and then, very suddenly, a downpour!”

      
Mrs. Bennet frowned, but Elizabeth chose to ignore it. 

      
“You must admit, Mama, it was very fortunate to have three officers to escort us home,” she continued. “How wonderful would it be to have two more marriages to celebrate at Christmastide?”

      
Lydia laughed loudly, while Kitty’s cheeks pinkened as she looked down at her plate.

      
“Do not be ridiculous,” Mrs. Bennet snapped, but she did so with a quick smile, her ire easily abated with thoughts of more of her daughters finding husbands in quick succession. 

      
Elizabeth knew that she was concerned for the future, as she well should be. It was not an easy thing to navigate the waters of inheritance with a house full of daughters. They must rely on themselves—and a prudent match—to see them through. 

      
Jane’s eventual engagement to Mr. Bingley would provide Mrs. Bennet with the security she required for when her husband was gone from the world—but the other girls…

      
“Well, you must all plan to give those officers the first dance at the regimental ball,” Mrs. Bennet huffed. “To express your favor and gratitude.”

      
“Of course, Mama,” Kitty murmured. 

      
“I shall dance with whomever I like,” Lydia exclaimed. 

      
“As long as you dance with Mr. Denny first,” Mrs. Bennet said firmly. “I should not like you to have a flippant reputation, Lydia. There are far too many young ladies in Hertfordshire for you to behave as such without a fear of… losing your place!”

      
“Losing my place,” Lydia snorted. “Mama, that will never happen. I am far too well loved to be set aside by one of the borning young ladies who populate this place!”

      
Mrs. Bennet’s brow furrowed, but she did not argue with her youngest daughter. It was a well known fact that Lydia was a popular dance partner at every event, but Elizabeth often wondered how long that would last once she chose a husband—or what might happen if the scandal Lydia flirted with made the decision for her.

      
But Lydia was young and foolish, and such things would soon pass by the wayside. Perhaps once Jane were married Lydia would begin to think of her own future.

      
It was possible. 

      
Doubtful… but still possible. 

      
“Well, there is a great deal of work to be done before the ball,” Mrs. Bennet huffed. “Kitty, your pink gown will have to be re-hemmed, and I do not know why you have brought home such a dark blue ribbon!”

      
“Mrs. Guilford suggested it,” Kitty replied softly. 

      
“That woman would say anything to make a sale,” Mrs. Bennet huffed. 

      
“And I will not be wearing pink,” Kitty said somewhat more firmly than before. “Lizzy said that she will help me—”

      
“But Lizzy will be too busy making ribbon roses for my gown,” Lydia interjected. 

      
Elizabeth set down her fork. “I shall help you with the ribbon roses,” she said. “You will not make me your servant for the sake of a few roses that you know very well how to make yourself.”

      
Lydia grumbled and pushed a forkful of potatoes into her mouth.

      
Jane had observed everything silently and Elizabeth wondered what her sister was thinking. The regimental ball would not be of any interest to her now that Mr. Bingley’s attentions had been directed toward her. 

      
“I shall be happy to assist Kitty,” Jane said with a smile. “The regimental ball is ever so exciting, is it not?”

      
“Especially with all of the new officers in town,” Lydia agreed readily. Her grin was bright as she leaned forward and placed her elbows upon the table. “Do you think I might be able to dance with all of them?”

      
“I daresay you might be able to,” Jane said. “You do have so much… energy.”

      
“I find balls invigorating,” Lydia laughed. “While the other ladies are sitting down to rest, I shall happily dance all the more!”

      
“Will you be coming to the regimental ball,” Kitty asked excitedly.

      
“Why would Jane come,” Lydia laughed. “She has Mr. Bingley to dance with whenever she likes.”

      
“Hush,” Mrs. Bennet said. “Your chatter has given me a headache. Finish your supper and then come into the parlor. We have a great deal of work to do, and there is very little time!”

      
The meal was completed in a relative silence that Elizabeth was grateful for. Before that day she had not quite decided whether or not she would attend the regimental ball, but after meeting Mr. Wickham, she had somewhat changed her mind. 

      
The orange ribbons she had chosen would, indeed, look striking in her hair, and no other young lady would dare deviate from the expected palette of pink, purple, or blue. 

      
Mr. Wickham was charming enough; he could be diverting company. 

      
      
In the parlor, Jane sat beside Elizabeth upon the couch.  While Elizabeth  worked at Lydia’s ribbon roses, Jane removed the old hems from the gown Kitty had chosen for the ball.

      
Elizabeth had promised to make two sections of roses and leaves to be applied to the bodice, but only if Lydia did the rest of the work. Her youngest sister’s stitches were large and a bit haphazard, but she would have to learn sometime. Her elder sisters would not always be around to do every bit of stitching that was required. 

      
“Will you come to tea at Netherfield Park this week?” Jane murmured. 

      
Elizabeth let out a heavy sigh. “Perhaps. As long as Mr. Darcy will not be present.”

      
“Gentlemen are rarely present at ladies’ teas,” Jane said with a smile. “And, besides, how bad could he really be? With a friend like Mr. Bingley—”

      
“Perhaps Mr. Bingley has poor judgment when it comes to making friends.”

      
Elizabeth regretted her words the instant they left her mouth. “Jane, I did not mean—”

      
“I know you did not,” Jane replied. “You are still angry with him. He was very rude, and has not taken the opportunity to apologize. You have every right to be cross with him, but perhaps you might make an effort to give him a chance to redeem himself? Everyone who meets you has no choice but to adore you.”

      
 “Miss Bingley does not agree,” Elizabeth murmured. 

      
“Then you should come to tea at Netherfield Park more often to better make her acquaintance,” Jane said. “If I am to be engaged to her brother, she will have to learn to love my sister.”

      
“As I shall be your constant companion after your marriage, I should think so,” Elizabeth said. “Perhaps she would change her attitude if she knew that I would always be within earshot?”

      
Jane pressed the back of her hand against her mouth to smother her laughter. “Elizabeth Anne Bennet, is that a threat?”

      
Elizabeth concentrated on her stitching. “Perhaps,” she replied lightly. 

      
“Say you will come to tea this week,” Jane pressed. She leaned against Elizabeth’s shoulder. “It will not be a hardship. And there will be lemon tarts.”

      
Elizabeth frowned. Lemon tarts were her weakness and Jane knew it well. 

      
“Fine.”

      
“You will come?”

      
Elizabeth nudged her sister back. “I shall think on it.”

      
Jane’s smile was one of victory as she tore a strip of ribbon from the hem of Kitty’s gown and dropped it into the basket of scraps at her feet. 

      
“That is good enough for me.”

      
“Let us see if we shall survive the regimental ball with our reputation intact,” Elizabeth said. “Then I shall see about turning Miss Bingley into an ally instead of a viper ready to strike.”

      
“She is not like that,” Jane murmured and then grimaced as she saw the expression upon Elizabeth’s face. “At least, I do not think she is.”

      
“We can only hope.”

      
Jane was silent and Elizabeth worried that she had been too harsh in her assessment—but there was something about Miss Caroline Bingley that did not sit well with her, though she could not determine what it might be.

      
Perhaps she was being too sensitive. But could the same thought be applied to Mr. Darcy and his rudeness?
